summary: The MIKEY key management scheme's existing modes do not suit deployments with a centralized key management service. This document defines new ticket-based MIKEY modes for those deployments. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Multimedia Internet KEYing with tickets (MIKEY-TICKET) adds a way to distribute keys for media sessions. An initiator obtains a ticket from a Key Management Service (KMS) and sends it to a responder, which obtains the session keys.

questions: how does mikey use a key management service
what is key forking in mikey
what are the mikey ticket modes
subtitle: Ticket-based MIKEY modes let a central service distribute media-session keys.

tldr.problem: Existing MIKEY modes use direct peer negotiation or pre-distributed credentials and do not fit every deployment built around a central key-management service.
tldr.mechanism: An Initiator can request keys and a ticket from a Key Management Service, transfer the ticket to a Responder, and let the Responder resolve it; some exchanges can be omitted depending on the ticket policy.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6043 is Informational and the supplied metadata says RFC 6309 updates it.

today: RFC 6043 is an Informational RFC published in March 2011 and has been updated by RFC 6309. It defines ticket-based modes for MIKEY key distribution.

sections.title: Why Add Tickets to MIKEY
sections.content:
The existing MIKEY modes rely on peers negotiating directly or on credentials distributed in advance. RFC 6043 adds modes for deployments that use a trusted Key Management Service (KMS).

The ticket identifies and delivers keys over an untrusted network. The design also supports situations where the Initiator does not know the exact Responder when it first contacts the KMS.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket method lets a central service provide key information when participants need it. The initiator can start before the final responder is known.

sections.title: Tickets, Forking and Central Key Management
sections.content:
A ticket may contain keys or refer to keys stored by the KMS. If it contains keys, the ticket data must be protected for confidentiality and integrity.

Forking sends a request to multiple possible endpoints. Key forking modifies keys so they are cryptographically unique for the responding endpoint. The RFC notes that a centralized KMS can become a single point of security failure.
sections.plainLanguage: A ticket can carry keys or point to keys held by the service. Key forking allows the service to bind keys to the endpoint that answers.

sections.title: Three Exchanges and Four Modes
sections.content:
MIKEY-TICKET involves an Initiator, a Responder and a KMS. Its possible exchanges are Ticket Request, Ticket Transfer and Ticket Resolve; a full mode uses all three, but the exchanges vary according to which parties hold the ticket-protection key.

If the KMS alone holds that key, both peers contact it. If the Responder can open the ticket, Ticket Resolve can be omitted; if the Initiator can create the ticket, Ticket Request can be omitted; if Initiator and Responder share the key, both can be omitted.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has three exchanges involving the initiator, responder and key service. A mode can omit an exchange when a party already has the ticket-protection key.

sections.title: Requesting, Transferring and Resolving a Ticket
sections.content:
In Ticket Request, the Initiator asks the KMS for keys and a ticket. The Initiator then sends the ticket to the Responder in Ticket Transfer; the transfer message is protected by a MIKEY Protection Key encoded in the ticket.

If needed, the Responder sends Ticket Resolve to the KMS and receives the ticket's keys. The Responder then sends a transfer response to the Initiator. A ticket may be reused for several transfers when its policy allows reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: The initiator can request a ticket, send it to the responder and let the responder obtain keys from the service. The exchanges depend on the ticket policy and keys already held.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Risks
sections.content:
The RFC says all keys, including keys protecting tickets, MUST be at least 128 bits. Random values used in key derivation help counter offline pre-computation attacks, and parties must authenticate before the KMS performs work.

The memo warns that optional features add complexity and encourages protocol designers to define strict profiles. It recommends rate limits and access-control lists to reduce denial-of-service risk and requires replay protections for messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The service must authenticate participants before processing requests, and keys must meet the minimum length in the RFC. Strict option profiles can limit complexity.
